title: Ἀμφίνομος καὶ Πηνελόπεια
titleEn: Amphinomus’s Warning and Penelope’s Appearance — Odyssey 18.108–214
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, wallet on his shoulder, goes back to the threshold while the suitors mock him with a wish that Zeus grant him his heart’s desire, and Amphinomus brings him bread and a golden cup. Odysseus answers him kindly and then warns him, in the form of a lesson on the frailty of mortals and the folly of those who forget the gods, that the master of the house is close and that the suitors will not part from him without blood. Amphinomus goes away troubled, but Athena has already bound him to die at Telemachus’s hands. Athena then puts into Penelope’s mind a wish to show herself to the suitors, and Penelope, after Eurynome’s advice, refuses to wash and anoint herself, saying that the gods ruined her beauty when her husband left. Athena puts her to sleep and makes her taller, whiter and more beautiful, and on waking she prays for a gentle death. She comes down with two handmaids and stands by the doorpost, and the suitors are weak at the knees with desire.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἀεικέα βάλλετο πήρην,
πυκνὰ ῥωγαλέην·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai amph’ ōmoisin aeikea balleto pērēn,
pykna rhōgaleēn·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and about his shoulders an unseemly wallet he threw,
thickly torn;
sentences.i: So he said, and slung an unseemly wallet about his shoulders, torn in many places;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is a formula, ‘he spoke, and’, with ἦ from ἠμί ‘say’ and ῥα the particle. βάλλετο is the imperfect middle of βάλλω, ‘threw about himself’. ἀεικέα ‘unseemly’ and ῥωγαλέην ‘torn’ both agree with πήρην ‘wallet’, and πυκνά is an adverb, ‘thickly, in many places’. The two lines stand also at 17.197–198, and the wallet is the one Odysseus was given at 13.437–438. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ στρόφος ἦεν ἀορτήρ.
sentences.tr: en de strophos ēen aortēr.
sentences.l: and on it a twisted cord was, for a strap.
sentences.i: and on it was a twisted cord to serve as a strap.
sentences.n: ἐν δέ is the adverb ‘and on it’, pointing to the wallet. στρόφος ‘twisted cord’ and ἀορτήρ ‘strap’ stand side by side, the cord being the strap. ἦεν is Homer’s ἦν ‘was’. These words end 13.438 and 17.198 in the same way.

sentences.t: ἂψ δ’ ὅ γ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο·
sentences.tr: aps d’ ho g’ ep’ oudon iōn kat’ ar’ hezeto·
sentences.l: And back, then, he, to the threshold going, sat down;
sentences.i: Then he went back to the threshold and sat down;
sentences.n: ἂψ δ’ ὅ γ’ is ‘and back he’: ἂψ is ‘back’, and ὅ γε is ‘he’, the ‘article’ used as a pronoun. ἐπ’ οὐδόν is ‘to the threshold’, with ἰών, the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. κατ’ … ἕζετο is a tmesis for κατέζετο, ‘sat down’, from ἕζομαι, with ἄρα ‘then’ between the two halves. The same opening stands at 17.466, where he also goes back to the threshold.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἴσαν εἴσω
ἡδὺ γελώοντες καὶ δεικανόωντ’ ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.tr:
toi d’ isan eisō
hēdy gelōontes kai deikanoōnt’ epeessi·
sentences.l:
and they went in
sweetly laughing and greeting him with words:
sentences.i: and they went in, laughing sweetly, and greeted him with these words:
sentences.n: τοί ‘they’ is the pronoun, the suitors. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, ‘went’, and εἴσω is ‘inside’. ἡδύ ‘sweetly’ is adverbial, and γελώοντες is the participle of γελάω with its vowels uncontracted (Attic γελῶντες). δεικανόωντ’ is the elided imperfect middle δεικανόωντο, ‘were greeting’, from a rare verb of greeting with a gesture; here the greeting is mockery, and the unit ends on the ano teleia that opens their speech.

sentences.t:
Ζεύς τοι δοίη, ξεῖνε, καὶ ἀθάνατοι θεοὶ ἄλλοι,
ὅττι μάλιστ’ ἐθέλεις καί τοι φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ,
ὃς τοῦτον τὸν ἄναλτον ἀλητεύειν ἀπέπαυσας
ἐν δήμῳ·
sentences.tr:
Zeus toi doiē, xeine, kai athanatoi theoi alloi,
hotti malist’ etheleis kai toi philon epleto thymōi,
hos touton ton analton alēteuein apepausas
en dēmōi·
sentences.l:
“May Zeus give you, stranger, and the other immortal gods,
what most you wish, and what to you dear has come to be in your heart,
you who this insatiable one from wandering
in the land have stopped;
sentences.i: “May Zeus grant you, stranger, and the other immortal gods, what you most wish, and what is dear to your heart, you who have stopped this insatiable fellow from wandering about the land;
sentences.n: The suitors greet Odysseus with a wish that is meant as a joke. δοίη is the aorist optative of δίδωμι, ‘may he give’, and τοι is ‘to you’ (Attic σοι). ὅττι is ὅ τι ‘what’ (‘whatever’), and ἔπλετο is the aorist of πέλομαι, ‘has come to be’. ὃς … ἀπέπαυσας is ‘you who have stopped’, with τοῦτον τὸν ἄναλτον ‘this insatiable one’ (Irus) as object and the infinitive ἀλητεύειν ‘from wandering as a vagrant’; ἐν δήμῳ is ‘in the land’.

sentences.t:
τάχα γάρ μιν ἀνάξομεν ἤπειρόνδε
εἰς Ἔχετον βασιλῆα, βροτῶν δηλήμονα πάντων.
sentences.tr:
tacha gar min anaxomen ēpeironde
eis Echeton basilēa, brotōn dēlēmona pantōn.
sentences.l:
for soon him we will take up to the mainland,
to Echetus the king, bane of all mortals.”
sentences.i: for we shall soon take him off to the mainland, to King Echetus, the bane of all mortals.”
sentences.n: ἀνάξομεν is the future of ἀνάγω ‘lead up’, used for taking a person away, as by sea; μιν is ‘him’, Irus. ἤπειρόνδε is ‘to the mainland’, with the direction-ending -δε. βασιλῆα is the epic accusative (Attic βασιλέα). The second line is Antinous’s own threat to Irus at 18.85, here turned by the suitors into a jest; δηλήμων ‘bane’ is one who does harm.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν, χαῖρεν δὲ κλεηδόνι δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephan, chairen de kleēdoni dios Odysseus.
sentences.l: So then they spoke, and rejoiced at the omen, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and heavenly Odysseus rejoiced at the omen.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’, the plural of ὣς φάτο; ἔφαν is the imperfect of φημί (= ἔφασαν). χαῖρεν is an unaugmented past of χαίρω. κλεηδών is an ‘omen’, a chance word that is heard as a sign (from κλέος ‘report’); the suitors speak in mockery, but Odysseus takes their wish for his good as a sign. δῖος is the stock epithet ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἄρα οἱ μεγάλην παρὰ γαστέρα θῆκεν,
ἐμπλείην κνίσης τε καὶ αἵματος·
sentences.tr:
Antinoos d’ ara hoi megalēn para gastera thēken,
empleiēn knisēs te kai haimatos·
sentences.l:
And Antinous then beside him a great belly set,
full of fat and of blood;
sentences.i: Antinous set a great paunch beside him, full of fat and blood;
sentences.n: οἱ ‘beside him’ is the dative of the pronoun, Odysseus, and παρά is an adverb tied to θῆκεν by tmesis (παραθῆκεν ‘set beside’). γαστήρ is the stomach of an animal, stuffed and roasted, one of the goats’ paunches of the prize at 44–45; ἐμπλείην ‘full’ is its adjective, with κνίσης τε καὶ αἵματος ‘of fat and of blood’ in the genitive of fullness. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Ἀμφίνομος δὲ
ἄρτους ἐκ κανέοιο δύω παρέθηκεν ἀείρας
καὶ δέπαϊ χρυσέῳ δειδίσκετο, φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr:
Amphinomos de
artous ek kaneoio dyō parethēken aeiras
kai depaï chryseōi deidisketo, phōnēsen te·
sentences.l:
and Amphinomus
two loaves from the basket set beside him, having lifted them,
and in a golden cup pledged him, and spoke:
sentences.i: and Amphinomus lifted two loaves from the basket and set them beside him, and pledged him in a golden cup, and said:
sentences.n: ἄρτους … δύω is ‘two loaves’ (δύω = δύο), and ἐκ κανέοιο ‘from the basket’ has the epic genitive in -οιο (Attic κανοῦ). παρέθηκεν ἀείρας is ‘set beside, having lifted’, the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’. δειδίσκετο is the imperfect middle of a rare verb of greeting or pledging with a cup, ‘pledged’, taken here from the context; δέπαϊ χρυσέῳ is ‘in a golden cup’, dative of the cup. φώνησέν τε is ‘and spoke’.

sentences.t:
χαῖρε, πάτερ ὦ ξεῖνε, γένοιτό τοι ἔς περ ὀπίσσω
ὄλβος·
sentences.tr:
chaire, pater ō xeine, genoito toi es per opissō
olbos·
sentences.l:
“Welcome, father, O stranger; may there come to you, even hereafter,
prosperity;
sentences.i: “Welcome, stranger, my father; may prosperity come to you at least in the time ahead;
sentences.n: χαῖρε, ξεῖνε ‘Welcome, stranger’ is the greeting to a guest, and πάτερ ὦ ξεῖνε is a courteous address to an older stranger: ‘father’ implies no kinship. γένοιτο is the aorist optative of γίγνομαι in a wish, ‘may it come to be’; τοι is ‘to you’. ἔς περ ὀπίσσω is ‘at least for the time to come’, and ὄλβος is ‘prosperity’, a settled state of having enough. The contrast with νῦν ‘now’ comes in the next unit.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ μὲν νῦν γε κακοῖς ἔχεαι πολέεσσι.
sentences.tr: atar men nyn ge kakois echeai poleessi.
sentences.l: but now, at least, you are held by many evils.”
sentences.i: but for the present you are beset by many evils.”
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ μὲν νῦν γε is ‘but now, at least’, and sets the present against the hoped-for ὄλβος. ἔχεαι is the middle of ἔχω with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic ἔχῃ); with a dative it means ‘be held by, be beset by’. κακοῖς … πολέεσσι is the dative plural, ‘by many evils’, where πολέεσσι is the epic form of πολλοῖς.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula, met before. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the present middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, and προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to, address’. πολύμητις is the stock epithet of Odysseus, ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις ‘cunning, craft’), translated each time.

sentences.t: Ἀμφίνομ’, ἦ μάλα μοι δοκέεις πεπνυμένος εἶναι·
sentences.tr: Amphinom’, ē mala moi dokeeis pepnymenos einai·
sentences.l: “Amphinomus, truly very to me you seem to be prudent;
sentences.i: “Amphinomus, you seem to me truly a prudent man;
sentences.n: Ἀμφίνομ’ is the vocative with its last vowel dropped. ἦ μάλα is an emphatic ‘truly, indeed’; ἦ here is the particle of assertion, not the verb ‘he said’ of 108. δοκέεις is uncontracted (Attic δοκεῖς), and δοκέεις μοι … εἶναι is ‘you seem to me to be’. πεπνυμένος is the word for prudence, ‘prudent’, the epithet Telemachus carries.

sentences.t:
τοίου γὰρ καὶ πατρός, ἐπεὶ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἄκουον,
Νῖσον Δουλιχιῆα ἐΰν τ’ ἔμεν ἀφνειόν τε·
sentences.tr:
toiou gar kai patros, epei kleos esthlon akouon,
Nison Doulichiēa eÿn t’ emen aphneion te·
sentences.l:
for of such a father too you are, since good fame I used to hear
that Nisus the Dulichian both good was and rich;
sentences.i: for you come of such a father too, since I used to hear a good name given to Nisus of Dulichium, that he was both a good man and a rich one;
sentences.n: τοίου … πατρός is a genitive of origin with ‘you are’ understood, ‘you are of such a father’; the next line says who he is. κλέος ἐσθλόν is ‘good fame’, a good name. Νῖσον is the accusative subject of the infinitive ἔμεν (Attic εἶναι), ‘that Nisus was’; Δουλιχιῆα is the Ionic accusative of Δουλιχιεύς, ‘Dulichian’, and ἐΰν is the accusative of ἐΰς ‘good’. ἀφνειός is ‘rich’.

sentences.t: τοῦ σ’ ἔκ φασι γενέσθαι, ἐπητῇ δ’ ἀνδρὶ ἔοικας.
sentences.tr: tou s’ ek phasi genesthai, epētēi d’ andri eoikas.
sentences.l: from him, they say, you were born, and to a man ready of speech you are like.
sentences.i: they say you were born of him, and you are like a man who is ready of speech.
sentences.n: τοῦ σ’ ἔκ is ἐκ τοῦ σε with the preposition placed after its pronoun, which the accent on ἔκ shows: ‘from him you’. φασι ‘they say’ takes the infinitive γενέσθαι ‘to have been born’. ἐπητῇ is the dative of ἐπητής, an adjective whose sense is only approximately known; ‘ready of speech’ is the traditional gloss, taken here. ἔοικας is the perfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative ἀνδρί.

sentences.t: τοὔνεκά τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δὲ σύνθεο καί μευ ἄκουσον·
sentences.tr: touneka toi ereō, sy de syntheo kai meu akouson·
sentences.l: For that reason I will tell you, and you, take it in, and hear me:
sentences.i: That is why I will tell you, and you must take it in and hear me:
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα, ‘for that reason’, and ἐρέω is the future of λέγω, ‘I will tell’. σύνθεο is the aorist middle imperative of συντίθημι, ‘put together in your mind, take in’, with the uncontracted ending -εο. καί μευ ἄκουσον is ‘and hear me’, ἄκουσον taking the genitive μευ (= μου).

sentences.t:
οὐδὲν ἀκιδνότερον γαῖα τρέφει ἀνθρώποιο,
πάντων ὅσσα τε γαῖαν ἔπι πνείει τε καὶ ἕρπει.
sentences.tr:
ouden akidnoteron gaia trephei anthrōpoio,
pantōn hossa te gaian epi pneiei te kai herpei.
sentences.l:
Nothing slighter does the earth nourish than man,
of all as many things as on the earth breathe and creep.
sentences.i: The earth nourishes nothing slighter than man, of all the creatures that breathe and move upon it.
sentences.n: ἀκιδνότερον is the comparative of ἀκιδνός, ‘weak, insignificant’, a rare word of which the derivation is not known; ‘slighter’ is the rendering already used for the same word at 5.217 and 8.169. ἀνθρώποιο is the epic genitive in -οιο (Attic ἀνθρώπου), the genitive of comparison, ‘than man’. ὅσσα τε … πνείει τε καὶ ἕρπει is ‘as many things as breathe and creep’: a neuter plural with a singular verb, πνείει uncontracted (Attic πνεῖ), and the epic τε marks a general truth. γαῖαν ἔπι is ἐπὶ γαῖαν with the preposition after its noun.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ ποτέ φησι κακὸν πείσεσθαι ὀπίσσω,
ὄφρ’ ἀρετὴν παρέχωσι θεοὶ καὶ γούνατ’ ὀρώρῃ·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar pote phēsi kakon peisesthai opissō,
ophr’ aretēn parechōsi theoi kai gounat’ orōrēi·
sentences.l:
For never, he says, will he suffer evil hereafter,
so long as the gods furnish excellence and his knees are stirring;
sentences.i: For as long as the gods grant him excellence and his knees keep moving, he says he will never suffer evil in time to come;
sentences.n: The subject is any man, from ἀνθρώποιο in the line before. φησι ‘he says’ takes the future infinitive πείσεσθαι ‘will suffer’ (πάσχω), and οὐ μέν … ποτέ is ‘never indeed’. ὄφρα ‘so long as’ takes the present subjunctive παρέχωσι ‘furnish’ (παρέχω) with no ἄν, as epic allows; ἀρετή is ‘excellence’. γούνατ’ ὀρώρῃ is the perfect subjunctive of ὄρνυμι with a neuter plural subject: ‘his knees are stirring’, a figure for being alive and fit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ λυγρὰ θεοὶ μάκαρες τελέσωσι,
καὶ τὰ φέρει ἀεκαζόμενος τετληότι θυμῷ·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē kai lygra theoi makares telesōsi,
kai ta pherei aekazomenos tetlēoti thymōi·
sentences.l:
but when even grievous things the blessed gods bring to pass,
these things too he bears, much against his will, with enduring heart;
sentences.i: but when the blessed gods bring grievous things to pass as well, he bears these too, much against his will, with an enduring heart;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καί is ‘but when even’. λυγρά is a neuter plural used as a noun, ‘grievous things’, and τελέσωσι the aorist subjunctive of τελέω ‘bring to pass’, without ἄν as in a general clause. τὰ is ‘these things’, the ‘article’ as a pronoun. ἀεκαζόμενος is ‘much against his will’, from ἀέκων ‘unwilling’; τετληότι is the perfect participle of τλάω ‘endure’, in the dative agreeing with θυμῷ, as in ‘with enduring heart’.

sentences.t:
τοῖος γὰρ νόος ἐστὶν ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων
οἷον ἐπ’ ἦμαρ ἄγησι πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε.
sentences.tr:
toios gar noos estin epichthoniōn anthrōpōn
hoion ep’ ēmar agēsi patēr andrōn te theōn te.
sentences.l:
For such is the mind of men upon the earth
as the day that the father of men and of gods brings upon them.
sentences.i: For the mind of men who live on the earth is just such as the day that the father of men and of gods brings upon them.
sentences.n: τοῖος … οἷον is ‘such … as’. ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων is ‘men upon the earth’. ἐπ’ … ἄγησι is probably a tmesis for ἐπάγῃσι, ‘brings upon’, with ἦμαρ ‘day’ as object and the subjunctive (Attic ἐπάγῃ) without ἄν; it could also be read ἐπ’ ἦμαρ ‘for the day’. The sense is that a man’s mind follows the fortune of the day that is sent him. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε is the stock title of Zeus.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐγώ ποτ’ ἔμελλον ἐν ἀνδράσιν ὄλβιος εἶναι,
πολλὰ δ’ ἀτάσθαλ’ ἔρεξα βίῃ καὶ κάρτεϊ εἴκων,
πατρί τ’ ἐμῷ πίσυνος καὶ ἐμοῖσι κασιγνήτοισι.
sentences.tr:
kai gar egō pot’ emellon en andrasin olbios einai,
polla d’ atasthal’ erexa biēi kai karteï eikōn,
patri t’ emōi pisynos kai emoisi kasignētoisi.
sentences.l:
For I too once was about to be prosperous among men,
and many wanton deeds I did, to force and might yielding,
to my father trusting, and to my brothers.
sentences.i: For I too was once about to be prosperous among men, and I did many wanton deeds, giving way to force and might, trusting in my father and in my brothers.
sentences.n: ἔμελλον with εἶναι is ‘was about to be’, and ὄλβιος is ‘prosperous’, the adjective of ὄλβος. ἀτάσθαλα is a neuter plural used as a noun, ‘wanton deeds’, and ἔρεξα is the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’. εἴκων ‘yielding’ takes the datives βίῃ and κάρτεϊ, where κάρτος is an Ionic form of κράτος ‘might’. πίσυνος ‘trusting, relying’ takes the dative πατρί and the epic κασιγνήτοισι (-οισι). Odysseus gives himself the history of a man who once prospered and abused his power.

sentences.t:
τῷ μή τίς ποτε πάμπαν ἀνὴρ ἀθεμίστιος εἴη,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε σιγῇ δῶρα θεῶν ἔχοι, ὅττι διδοῖεν.
sentences.tr:
tōi mē tis pote pampan anēr athemistios eiē,
all’ ho ge sigēi dōra theōn echoi, hotti didoien.
sentences.l:
Therefore let no man ever at all be lawless,
but let him, for his part, in silence hold the gifts of the gods, whatever they give.
sentences.i: So let no man ever be lawless; let him keep in silence whatever gifts the gods may give.
sentences.n: τῷ is the dative of the pronoun used as ‘therefore’. μὴ … εἴη and ἔχοι are optatives of wish, ‘let him not be’, ‘let him hold’. ἀθεμίστιος ‘lawless’ is from θέμις, ‘what custom and right allow’, a kinsman of the ἀθέμιστος ‘lawless’ used of the Cyclopes. ὅ γε is ‘he’; σιγῇ is a dative of manner, ‘in silence’. ὅττι διδοῖεν is ‘whatever they may give’, an indefinite relative with the optative of δίδωμι, the gods being the subject.

sentences.t:
οἷ’ ὁρόω μνηστῆρας ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωντας,
κτήματα κείροντας καὶ ἀτιμάζοντας ἄκοιτιν
ἀνδρός, ὃν οὐκέτι φημὶ φίλων καὶ πατρίδος αἴης
δηρὸν ἀπέσσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
hoi’ horoō mnēstēras atasthala mēchanoōntas,
ktēmata keirontas kai atimazontas akoitin
andros, hon ouketi phēmi philōn kai patridos aiēs
dēron apessesthai·
sentences.l:
Such things I see the suitors devising, wanton deeds,
shearing away possessions and dishonouring the wife
of a man who, I say, no longer from his dear ones and fatherland
for long will be away;
sentences.i: I see the suitors devising wanton deeds, wasting possessions and dishonouring the wife of a man who, I say, will not be away from his dear ones and his fatherland much longer;
sentences.n: οἷ’ is οἷα, ‘such things as’, introducing what he sees. μηχανόωντας is the uncontracted participle of μηχανάομαι ‘devise’ (Attic μηχανωμένους), with ἀτάσθαλα ‘wanton deeds’ as object. κείροντας ‘shearing’ is the verb for cutting a fleece or a crop, here ‘wasting’, with κτήματα ‘possessions’; ἄκοιτιν is ‘wife’. ἀνδρός is the absent husband, and the speaker is that man, naming himself as a third person. φημί takes the future infinitive ἀπέσσεσθαι ‘will be away’, with οὐκέτι δηρόν ‘no longer for long’.

sentences.t: μάλα δὲ σχεδόν.
sentences.tr: mala de schedon.
sentences.l: and very near.
sentences.i: and very near at hand.
sentences.n: μάλα δὲ σχεδόν is a short clause with no verb: ‘and very near’. σχεδόν is ‘near’, and the Greek leaves it open whether the nearness is of place or of time; the thing that is near, his return, has to be supplied from the clause before. The unit is as short as the clause is.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά σε δαίμων
οἴκαδ’ ὑπεξαγάγοι, μηδ’ ἀντιάσειας ἐκείνῳ,
ὁππότε νοστήσειε φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
alla se daimōn
oikad’ hypexagagoi, mēd’ antiaseias ekeinōi,
hoppote nostēseie philēn es patrida gaian·
sentences.i: But may some power lead you away home, and may you not meet him when he comes back to his dear fatherland;
sentences.n: δαίμων is ‘some power’, an unnamed divine agency. ὑπεξαγάγοι is the aorist optative of ὑπεξάγω ‘lead out from under (danger)’, a wish; οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, with the ending -δε. μηδ’ ἀντιάσειας is the aorist optative of ἀντιάω ‘meet’ in a negative wish, taking the dative ἐκείνῳ ‘that man’, that is, the husband. ὁππότε νοστήσειε is ‘whenever he comes home’; φίλην … πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘his dear fatherland’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἀναιμωτί γε διακρινέεσθαι ὀΐω
μνηστῆρας καὶ κεῖνον, ἐπεί κε μέλαθρον ὑπέλθῃ.
sentences.tr:
ou gar anaimōti ge diakrineesthai oïō
mnēstēras kai keinon, epei ke melathron hypelthēi.
sentences.l:
For not without blood, I think, will they be parted,
the suitors and that man, when he comes beneath the roof.”
sentences.i: For I do not think the suitors and he will part without bloodshed, once he comes under the roof.”
sentences.n: ἀναιμωτί ‘without blood’ is an adverb from αἷμα. διακρινέεσθαι is the future infinitive of διακρίνω ‘separate’, in the middle ‘part from one another, settle it between them’, after ὀΐω ‘I think’. κεῖνον is ‘that man’ (Attic ἐκεῖνον). ἐπεί κε … ὑπέλθῃ is ‘once he has come under’, with the aorist subjunctive of ὑπέρχομαι; μέλαθρον is the roof-beam, then the roof, standing for the house.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, καὶ σπείσας ἔπιεν μελιηδέα οἶνον,
ἂψ δ’ ἐν χερσὶν ἔθηκε δέπας κοσμήτορι λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, kai speisas epien meliēdea oinon,
aps d’ en chersin ethēke depas kosmētori laōn.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and having poured a libation he drank the honey-sweet wine,
and back in the hands he put the cup, to the marshaller of the people.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and after pouring a libation he drank the honey-sweet wine, and put the cup back in the hands of the marshal of the people.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the speech-closing ‘So he spoke’. σπείσας is ‘having poured a libation’, with ἔπιεν ‘drank’; μελιηδέα οἶνον is ‘honey-sweet wine’. ἂψ … ἔθηκε is ‘put back’, and ἐν χερσίν ‘in the hands’ with the dative κοσμήτορι gives whose: ‘to the marshaller’. κοσμήτωρ λαῶν is a title of honour for a leader who sets the people in order (from κοσμέω ‘arrange’), used here of Amphinomus.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ βῆ διὰ δῶμα φίλον τετιημένος ἦτορ,
νευστάζων κεφαλῇ·
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē dia dōma philon tetiēmenos ētor,
neustazōn kephalēi·
sentences.l:
But he went through the house, grieved in his dear heart,
nodding with his head;
sentences.i: But Amphinomus went through the house, grieving in his heart, nodding his head;
sentences.n: ὁ is ‘he’, Amphinomus, and βῆ is the unaugmented aorist ‘went’. τετιημένος ἦτορ is ‘grieved in heart’, ἦτορ an accusative of respect, with φίλον ‘dear’ agreeing with ἦτορ across the word between. νευστάζων is the participle of νευστάζω, ‘nodding repeatedly’, and κεφαλῇ is a dative of means; the gesture is a sad shake or nod of the head. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: δὴ γὰρ κακὸν ὄσσετο θυμός.
sentences.tr: dē gar kakon osseto thymos.
sentences.l: for indeed evil his heart foresaw.
sentences.i: for his heart foresaw evil.
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, giving the reason for the grief and the nodding. ὄσσετο is the imperfect middle of ὄσσομαι ‘foresee, bode’, a Homeric word with no Attic equivalent; κακόν ‘evil’ is its object and θυμός ‘heart’ its subject.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς φύγε κῆρα·
sentences.tr: all’ oud’ hōs phyge kēra·
sentences.l: But not even so did he flee death-fate;
sentences.i: Yet even so he did not escape death;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὥς is ‘but not even so’; accented ὥς is the adverb ‘thus’. φύγε is the unaugmented aorist of φεύγω. κῆρα is the accusative of κήρ ‘death-fate’, a power of death, a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’. The unit ends at an ano teleia, and the rest of the sentence says why he could not escape.

sentences.t:
πέδησε δὲ καὶ τὸν Ἀθήνη
Τηλεμάχου ὑπὸ χερσὶ καὶ ἔγχεϊ ἶφι δαμῆναι.
sentences.tr:
pedēse de kai ton Athēnē
Tēlemachou hypo chersi kai encheï iphi damēnai.
sentences.l:
and Athena bound him too
to be subdued beneath the hands of Telemachus and by the spear, with force.
sentences.i: for Athena had fettered him as well, to be overcome by force at the hands of Telemachus and by his spear.
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’ with καί ‘too’, Amphinomus. πέδησε is the unaugmented aorist of πεδάω ‘bind, fetter’. δαμῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, giving the purpose or result of the binding. Τηλεμάχου ὑπὸ χερσί is ‘under the hands of Telemachus’, ἔγχεϊ the dative of ἔγχος ‘spear’ with the ending -εϊ, and ἶφι ‘by force’ the old instrumental of ἴς ‘force’. The line says in advance how Amphinomus will die.

sentences.t: ἂψ δ’ αὖτις κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐπὶ θρόνου ἔνθεν ἀνέστη.
sentences.tr: aps d’ autis kat’ ar’ hezet’ epi thronou enthen anestē.
sentences.l: And back again he sat down upon the chair from which he had risen.
sentences.i: He went back and sat down again on the chair he had risen from.
sentences.n: ἂψ … αὖτις is ‘back again’, two words for one idea. κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ is a tmesis for κατέζετο ‘sat down’. ἐπὶ θρόνου is ‘upon the chair’, and ἔνθεν ἀνέστη is ‘from where he had risen’: ἔνθεν is ‘from where’, with the ending -θεν of ‘from’, and ἀνέστη is the aorist of ἀνίστημι in its intransitive sense.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
κούρῃ Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
sentences.tr:
tēi d’ ar’ epi phresi thēke thea glaukōpis Athēnē,
kourēi Ikarioio, periphroni Pēnelopeiēi,
sentences.l:
And to her in her mind put the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
to the daughter of Icarius, to circumspect Penelope,
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, put it into the mind of the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope,
sentences.n: τῇ is ‘to her’, with κούρῃ Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ in apposition, ‘to her, the daughter of Icarius’. ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε is ‘put in her mind’; what she was to think is given in the next lines. Ἰκαρίοιο is a genitive in -οιο, and Πηνελοπείῃ the dative of Πηνελόπεια. The epithets are rendered each time: γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ and περίφρων ‘circumspect’. The unit ends at a comma, because the sentence is five lines long.

sentences.t:
μνηστήρεσσι φανῆναι, ὅπως πετάσειε μάλιστα
θυμὸν μνηστήρων ἰδὲ τιμήεσσα γένοιτο
μᾶλλον πρὸς πόσιός τε καὶ υἱέος ἢ πάρος ἦεν.
sentences.tr:
mnēstēressi phanēnai, hopōs petaseie malista
thymon mnēstērōn ide timēessa genoito
mallon pros posios te kai huieos ē paros ēen.
sentences.l:
to appear to the suitors, so that she might open wide, most of all,
the heart of the suitors, and become honoured
more with her husband and her son than before she was.
sentences.i: to show herself to the suitors, so that she might open the suitors’ hearts as wide as she could, and become more honoured in the eyes of her husband and her son than she had been before.
sentences.n: φανῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of φαίνω, ‘to appear, show oneself’. ὅπως … πετάσειε is a purpose clause with the aorist optative of πετάννυμι ‘spread out, open wide’; said of the heart it is a figure the line does not explain, and ‘open wide’ is taken literally. ἰδέ is ‘and’ (= καί). τιμήεσσα is the feminine of τιμήεις ‘honoured’; πρὸς πόσιός τε καὶ υἱέος is ‘in the eyes of her husband and son’; ἦεν is ἦν.

sentences.t: ἀχρεῖον δ’ ἐγέλασσεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr: achreion d’ egelassen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l: And idly she laughed, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: She gave an idle laugh, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: ἀχρεῖον is a neuter used as an adverb, ‘uselessly, to no purpose’, so the laugh is an empty one, with no mirth behind it. ἐγέλασσεν is the aorist of γελάω with the epic doubled σ. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the formula ‘spoke a word and called by name’, ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν a tmesis, and ἔφατ’ the elided imperfect ἔφατο; the one she names is Eurynome, in the first word of the speech.

sentences.t:
Εὐρυνόμη, θυμός μοι ἐέλδεται, οὔ τι πάρος γε,
μνηστήρεσσι φανῆναι, ἀπεχθομένοισί περ ἔμπης·
sentences.tr:
Eurynomē, thymos moi eeldetai, ou ti paros ge,
mnēstēressi phanēnai, apechthomenoisi per empēs·
sentences.l:
“Eurynome, my heart longs, not at all before now,
to appear to the suitors, though they are hateful, all the same;
sentences.i: “Eurynome, my heart longs, as it never did before, to show myself to the suitors, hateful though they are, all the same;
sentences.n: Penelope speaks to Eurynome, who is named housekeeper at 169. θυμός μοι ἐέλδεται is ‘my heart longs’, ἐέλδομαι being ‘long for’ with a prothetic ἐ-, and takes the infinitive φανῆναι ‘to appear’. οὔ τι πάρος γε is ‘not at all before’, the longing being new. ἀπεχθομένοισι is the dative plural participle of ἀπέχθομαι ‘be hateful’, agreeing with μνηστήρεσσι; περ makes it concessive, and ἔμπης is ‘all the same’.

sentences.t:
παιδὶ δέ κεν εἴποιμι ἔπος, τό κε κέρδιον εἴη,
μὴ πάντα μνηστῆρσιν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ὁμιλεῖν,
οἵ τ’ εὖ μὲν βάζουσι, κακῶς δ’ ὄπιθεν φρονέουσι.
sentences.tr:
paidi de ken eipoimi epos, to ke kerdion eiē,
mē panta mnēstērsin hyperphialoisin homilein,
hoi t’ eu men bazousi, kakōs d’ opithen phroneousi.
sentences.l:
and to my son I might say a word, which would be better,
not to mingle in everything with the overweening suitors,
who speak well, but think ill behind.”
sentences.i: and I would tell my son a word that would be better: not to keep company in everything with the overweening suitors, who speak well, but think ill behind one’s back.”
sentences.n: παιδί is ‘to my son’, Telemachus; εἴποιμι κε is the optative with κε, ‘I might say’, and τό κε κέρδιον εἴη is ‘which would be better’, κέρδιον being a comparative from κέρδος ‘gain’, ‘better, more profitable’. μὴ … ὁμιλεῖν is the content of the word, ‘not to mingle’, with πάντα ‘in everything’. ὑπερφιάλοισιν ‘overweening’ is the dative plural. βάζουσι is ‘speak’, φρονέουσι the uncontracted ‘think’, and ὄπιθεν is ‘behind’; the epic τε in οἵ τε marks a general description.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρυνόμη ταμίη πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aut’ Eurynomē tamiē pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l: Her then in turn Eurynome, the housekeeper, with a word addressed:
sentences.i: Then the housekeeper Eurynome spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula. τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘her then in turn’, with Εὐρυνόμη ταμίη ‘Eurynome, the housekeeper’. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is a tmesis for προσέειπεν ‘addressed’, with μῦθον ‘a word’ in between. The house rendering keeps ‘addressed’ for this verb and ‘in turn’ for αὖτε.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα, τέκος, κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: nai dē tauta ge panta, tekos, kata moiran eeipes.
sentences.l: “Yes, indeed, all this, at least, child, according to what is fitting you have spoken.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, child, all this you have said, as is fitting.
sentences.n: ναὶ δή is ‘yes indeed’, and ταῦτά γε πάντα ‘all this, at least’. τέκος is the vocative of τέκος ‘child’, the address of an old woman to a younger, and implies no kinship here. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘as is fitting’, literally ‘according to portion’. ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with the augment left unfused with the root’s first vowel (Attic εἶπες).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι καὶ σῷ παιδὶ ἔπος φάο μηδ’ ἐπίκευθε,
χρῶτ’ ἀπονιψαμένη καὶ ἐπιχρίσασα παρειάς·
sentences.tr:
all’ ithi kai sōi paidi epos phao mēd’ epikeuthe,
chrōt’ aponipsamenē kai epichrisasa pareias·
sentences.l:
But go, and to your son speak a word, and do not hide it,
having washed off your skin and anointed your cheeks;
sentences.i: But go, and tell your son the word, and do not keep it hidden, once you have washed your skin and anointed your cheeks;
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’. φάο is a present middle imperative of φημί, ‘speak!’, and μηδ’ ἐπίκευθε is ‘and do not hide’; ἔπος ‘word’ is the object of both. σῷ is ‘your’, the possessive adjective. χρῶτ’ ἀπονιψαμένη and ἐπιχρίσασα are aorist participles, the first middle (‘washed off your skin’), the second active (‘anointed’), with παρειάς ‘cheeks’ as object.

sentences.t:
μηδ’ οὕτω δακρύοισι πεφυρμένη ἀμφὶ πρόσωπα
ἔρχευ, ἐπεὶ κάκιον πενθήμεναι ἄκριτον αἰεί.
sentences.tr:
mēd’ houtō dakryoisi pephyrmenē amphi prosōpa
ercheu, epei kakion penthēmenai akriton aiei.
sentences.l:
and not thus with tears besmeared about your face
go, since worse it is to mourn without end, always.
sentences.i: and do not go like this, your face soaked with tears, since it is worse to grieve endlessly, always.
sentences.n: μηδ’ οὕτω … ἔρχευ is ‘and do not go thus’, ἔρχευ being the imperative of ἔρχομαι with the uncontracted ending -ευ. πεφυρμένη is the perfect passive participle of φύρω ‘mix’, here ‘soaked with’ the dative δακρύοισι; ἀμφὶ πρόσωπα ‘about the face’ has the plural πρόσωπα for one face. κάκιον is the comparative of κακός, ‘worse’. πενθήμεναι is an infinitive in -ήμεναι (Attic πενθεῖν), and ἄκριτον αἰεί is ‘without end, always’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν γάρ τοι παῖς τηλίκος, ὃν σὺ μάλιστα
ἠρῶ ἀθανάτοισι γενειήσαντα ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ēdē men gar toi pais tēlikos, hon sy malista
ērō athanatoisi geneiēsanta idesthai.
sentences.l:
For already your son is of such an age, whom you most of all
prayed to the immortals to see grown a beard.”
sentences.i: For your son is already of an age, the son you prayed to the immortals above all to see bearded.”
sentences.n: ἤδη … τηλίκος is ‘already of such an age’, with τοι ‘your’ (Attic σοι), a dative of the person concerned. ὃν σὺ μάλιστα ἠρῶ is ‘whom you most of all prayed’, where ἠρῶ is the contracted imperfect middle of ἀράομαι ‘pray’ (ἠράου, 2 sg.) and ἀθανάτοισι is the dative ‘to the immortals’. γενειήσαντα is the aorist participle of γενειάω ‘grow a beard’, agreeing with ὃν, and ἰδέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ὁράω ‘to see’.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula already met. τὴν δ’ αὖτε is ‘her then in turn’, and προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’ with the augment left unfused (Attic προσεῖπε); the house rendering ‘addressed’ goes with it, and περίφρων ‘circumspect’ is the stock epithet of Penelope.

sentences.t:
Εὐρυνόμη, μὴ ταῦτα παραύδα, κηδομένη περ,
χρῶτ’ ἀπονίπτεσθαι καὶ ἐπιχρίεσθαι ἀλοιφῇ·
sentences.tr:
Eurynomē, mē tauta parauda, kēdomenē per,
chrōt’ aponiptesthai kai epichriesthai aloiphēi·
sentences.l:
“Eurynome, do not speak soothingly of this, concerned though you are,
of washing off my skin and of anointing myself with ointment;
sentences.i: “Eurynome, do not talk to me soothingly of this, concerned as you are, of washing my skin and anointing myself with ointment;
sentences.n: μὴ ταῦτα παραύδα is ‘do not speak soothingly of this’; παραυδάω is ‘talk to, soothe’, here to urge a course by gentle words. κηδομένη περ is ‘although you are concerned’, with περ concessive. The infinitives ἀπονίπτεσθαι and ἐπιχρίεσθαι are middle, ‘wash oneself’ and ‘anoint oneself’, giving what Eurynome had urged at 172. ἀλοιφή is anything smeared on, ‘ointment’, fat or oil.

sentences.t:
ἀγλαΐην γὰρ ἐμοί γε θεοί, τοὶ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν,
ὤλεσαν, ἐξ οὗ κεῖνος ἔβη κοίλῃς ἐνὶ νηυσίν.
sentences.tr:
aglaïēn gar emoi ge theoi, toi Olympon echousin,
ōlesan, ex hou keinos ebē koilēis eni nēusin.
sentences.l:
For my splendour, for me at least, the gods who hold Olympus
destroyed, from the time that man went in hollow ships.
sentences.i: For the gods who hold Olympus destroyed my beauty, for me at least, from the day that man went off in hollow ships.
sentences.n: ἀγλαΐη is ‘splendour’, here Penelope’s beauty, and γάρ gives her reason for refusing. ἐμοί γε is ‘for me at least’. τοί is the relative ‘who’ in θεοί, τοὶ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν ‘the gods who hold Olympus’. ὤλεσαν is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’, and ἐξ οὗ ‘from the time when’. κεῖνος is ‘that man’ (Attic ἐκεῖνος), her husband, and κοίλῃς … νηυσίν is ‘in hollow ships’, with the dative ending shortened.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι Αὐτονόην τε καὶ Ἱπποδάμειαν ἄνωχθι
ἐλθέμεν, ὄφρα κέ μοι παρστήετον ἐν μεγάροισιν·
sentences.tr:
alla moi Autonoēn te kai Hippodameian anōchthi
elthemen, ophra ke moi parstēeton en megaroisin·
sentences.l:
But for me Autonoe and Hippodameia bid
to come, so that the two may stand by me in the halls;
sentences.i: But bid Autonoe and Hippodameia come to me, so that the two of them may stand beside me in the hall;
sentences.n: ἄνωχθι is the imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid, order’, a perfect with present sense, and takes the infinitive ἐλθέμεν (Attic ἐλθεῖν); μοι can go with the bidding, ‘for me’, as in the Greek line above, or with ‘come’, ‘to me’, as in the English. Αὐτονόην and Ἱπποδάμειαν are two women of the household. παρστήετον is a dual, ‘the two may stand by’, the subjunctive of παρίστημι with its vowels uncontracted; the dual fits the δύ’ ἀμφίπολοι ‘two handmaids’ of 207. ὄφρα κε takes the subjunctive, ‘so that’; ἐν μεγάροισιν is ‘in the hall’.

sentences.t: οἴη δ’ οὐκ εἴσειμι μετ’ ἀνέρας·
sentences.tr: oiē d’ ouk eiseimi met’ aneras·
sentences.l: and alone I will not go among the men;
sentences.i: for I will not go in among the men alone;
sentences.n: οἴη is the feminine of οἶος ‘alone’, nominative, saying that she goes by herself. εἴσειμι is the present of εἴσειμι (εἰς + εἶμι) with future sense, ‘I shall go in’. μετ’ ἀνέρας is ‘among the men’, with the epic accusative ἀνέρας (Attic ἄνδρας). The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line, and the reason follows.

sentences.t: αἰδέομαι γάρ.
sentences.tr: aideomai gar.
sentences.l: for I feel shame.”
sentences.i: for I am ashamed.”
sentences.n: αἰδέομαι is ‘I feel shame’, the verb of αἰδώς, the respect and shyness a person feels before others. Here it is her reason for not going among the suitors without company. γάρ ‘for’ gives that reason, and the two words close Penelope’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, γρηῢς δὲ διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
ἀγγελέουσα γυναιξὶ καὶ ὀτρυνέουσα νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, grēÿs de diek megaroio bebēkei
angeleousa gynaixi kai otryneousa neesthai.
sentences.l:
So then she spoke, and the old woman out through the hall had gone,
to bring word to the women and to urge them to come.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the old woman went out through the hall to carry the message to the women and to urge them to come.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is ‘so then she spoke’. γρηῢς is the old woman, Eurynome, the Homeric form of Attic γραῦς. διὲκ μεγάροιο is ‘out through the hall’, and βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω with a simple past force, ‘had gone, went’. ἀγγελέουσα and ὀτρυνέουσα are future participles of purpose, ‘to announce’ and ‘to urge’, and νέεσθαι the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι ‘come, go’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: enth’ aut’ all’ enoēse thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Then again another thing devised the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, thought of something else:
sentences.n: A formula, also at 2.382, 2.393 and 4.795. ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ is ‘then again’, marking a new act of the goddess, and ἄλλ’ is ἄλλο ‘another thing’, the object of ἐνόησε, the aorist of νοέω ‘think, devise’. The unit ends at an ano teleia, and the other thing follows. θεά ‘goddess’ and γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ keep their house renderings.

sentences.t:
κούρῃ Ἰκαρίοιο κατὰ γλυκὺν ὕπνον ἔχευεν,
εὗδε δ’ ἀνακλινθεῖσα, λύθεν δέ οἱ ἅψεα πάντα
αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ κλιντῆρι·
sentences.tr:
kourēi Ikarioio kata glykyn hypnon echeuen,
heude d’ anaklintheisa, lythen de hoi hapsea panta
autou eni klintēri·
sentences.i: she poured sweet sleep upon the daughter of Icarius, and she slept, leaning back, and all her limbs relaxed, there on her couch;
sentences.n: κατὰ … ἔχευεν is a tmesis for κατέχευεν ‘poured down’, the verb used for shedding a grace, so that the sleep is thought of as a liquid; κούρῃ Ἰκαρίοιο is Penelope, in the dative of the one on whom it is poured. The second line repeats 4.794, where sleep falls on Penelope as she lies thinking of her son; it is not Athena who sends it there, and the same Athena formula (ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε) follows at 4.795. ἀνακλινθεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of ἀνακλίνω, ‘having leaned back’, and λύθεν the unaugmented aorist passive of λύω, ‘were loosened’, with ἅψεα ‘limbs’ as subject. αὐτοῦ is ‘on the spot’, and κλιντήρ is a couch to recline on, from κλίνω.

sentences.t:
τέως δ’ ἄρα δῖα θεάων
ἄμβροτα δῶρα δίδου, ἵνα μιν θησαίατ’ Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
teōs d’ ara dia theaōn
ambrota dōra didou, hina min thēsaiat’ Achaioi.
sentences.l:
and meanwhile the heavenly-one of goddesses
deathless gifts was giving, so that the Achaeans might gaze at her.
sentences.i: and meanwhile Athena, heavenly even among goddesses, gave her deathless gifts, so that the Achaeans would gaze at her in wonder.
sentences.n: τέως is ‘meanwhile’, and δῖα θεάων is ‘heavenly one of the goddesses’, here Athena. ἄμβροτα is ‘deathless’, and δίδου the imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘was giving’. ἵνα μιν θησαίατ’ is a purpose clause with the aorist optative of θηέομαι ‘gaze at with wonder’, μιν ‘her’; Ἀχαιοί is the men of the hall. The gifts are those of the next lines.

sentences.t:
κάλλεϊ μέν οἱ πρῶτα προσώπατα καλὰ κάθηρεν
ἀμβροσίῳ, οἵῳ περ ἐϋστέφανος Κυθέρεια
χρίεται, εὖτ’ ἂν ἴῃ Χαρίτων χορὸν ἱμερόεντα·
sentences.tr:
kalleï men hoi prōta prosōpata kala kathēren
ambrosiōi, hoiōi per eÿstephanos Kythereia
chrietai, eut’ an iēi Charitōn choron himeroenta·
sentences.i: First she cleansed her beautiful face with an ambrosial beauty, such as fair-crowned Cytherea uses to anoint herself whenever she goes to the dance of the Graces, a dance full of longing;
sentences.n: κάλλεϊ … ἀμβροσίῳ is ‘with ambrosial beauty’, a divine beauty-preparation, the word for beauty serving as the name of the salve. προσώπατα καλά is ‘fine face’ in an epic plural, and κάθηρεν the unaugmented aorist of καθαίρω ‘cleanse’. οἵῳ περ … χρίεται is ‘such as she anoints herself with’. Κυθέρεια is Aphrodite, named from the island Cythera; ἐϋστέφανος is ‘fair-crowned’. εὖτ’ ἂν ἴῃ is ‘whenever she goes’, and ἱμερόεντα ‘full of longing’ agrees with χορόν.

sentences.t:
καί μιν μακροτέρην καὶ πάσσονα θῆκεν ἰδέσθαι,
λευκοτέρην δ’ ἄρα μιν θῆκε πριστοῦ ἐλέφαντος.
sentences.tr:
kai min makroterēn kai passona thēken idesthai,
leukoterēn d’ ara min thēke pristou elephantos.
sentences.l:
and her taller and stouter she made to look upon,
and whiter then she made her than sawn ivory.
sentences.i: and made her taller and stouter to look upon, and made her whiter than sawn ivory.
sentences.n: μιν is ‘her’, and θῆκεν … ἰδέσθαι ‘made to look upon’, with the aorist infinitive of respect. μακροτέρην, πάσσονα and λευκοτέρην are comparatives agreeing with μιν ‘her’ (the first and third are feminine forms): ‘taller, stouter, whiter’. πριστοῦ ἐλέφαντος is the genitive of comparison, ‘than sawn ivory’, πριστός being from πρίω ‘saw’. The first line is 8.20, where Athena makes Odysseus taller and stouter, except that the adjective there is the masculine μακρότερον.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς ἔρξασ’ ἀπεβήσετο δῖα θεάων,
ἦλθον δ’ ἀμφίπολοι λευκώλενοι ἐκ μεγάροιο
φθόγγῳ ἐπερχόμεναι·
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ hōs erxas’ apebēseto dia theaōn,
ēlthon d’ amphipoloi leukōlenoi ek megaroio
phthongōi eperchomenai·
sentences.i: When she had done this, Athena, heavenly even among goddesses, went away, and the white-armed attendants came out of the hall, approaching with a sound;
sentences.n: ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς ἔρξασ’ is ‘she, then, having so done’, ἔρξασα being the aorist participle of ῥέζω. ἀπεβήσετο is the aorist middle of ἀποβαίνω, ‘went away’. ἀμφίπολοι is ‘attendants’, women of the household, and λευκώλενοι ‘white-armed’. φθόγγῳ is a dative of manner, ‘with a sound, with voices’, and ἐπερχόμεναι ‘coming on’; it is their noise that rouses Penelope. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἀνῆκε,
καί ῥ’ ἀπομόρξατο χερσὶ παρειὰς φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr:
tēn de glykys hypnos anēke,
kai rh’ apomorxato chersi pareias phōnēsen te·
sentences.l:
and her sweet sleep released,
and she wiped off her cheeks with her hands and spoke:
sentences.i: and sweet sleep let her go, and she wiped her cheeks with her hands and spoke:
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘her’, and ἀνῆκε the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘release’, so that ‘sweet sleep let her go’. καί ῥ’ is καὶ ῥα ‘and then’, and ἀπομόρξατο is the aorist middle of ἀπομόργνυμι ‘wipe off from oneself’, with χερσί ‘with her hands’ and παρειάς ‘cheeks’, as one does on waking. φώνησέν τε is ‘and spoke’, the accent moving onto the verb before τε.

sentences.t: ἦ με μάλ’ αἰνοπαθῆ μαλακὸν περὶ κῶμ’ ἐκάλυψεν.
sentences.tr: ē me mal’ ainopathē malakon peri kōm’ ekalypsen.
sentences.l: “Truly, me, very fearsomely suffering, a soft slumber has covered over.
sentences.i: “A soft slumber has wrapped itself around me, so terribly afflicted as I am.
sentences.n: ἦ is the particle ‘truly’, not the verb of 108, and μάλα ‘very’ goes with αἰνοπαθῆ. αἰνοπαθῆ is accusative, agreeing with με; it is built on αἰνός ‘fearsome’ and the root of πάσχω ‘suffer’, ‘suffering terribly’. περί … ἐκάλυψεν is a tmesis for περικάλυψεν ‘covered round’, the aorist of καλύπτω, with κῶμα ‘deep sleep, slumber’ as subject and μαλακόν ‘soft’. She says nothing of Athena, who sent the sleep (188).

sentences.t:
αἴθε μοι ὣς μαλακὸν θάνατον πόροι Ἄρτεμις ἁγνὴ
αὐτίκα νῦν, ἵνα μηκέτ’ ὀδυρομένη κατὰ θυμὸν
αἰῶνα φθινύθω, πόσιος ποθέουσα φίλοιο
παντοίην ἀρετήν, ἐπεὶ ἔξοχος ἦεν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
aithe moi hōs malakon thanaton poroi Artemis hagnē
autika nyn, hina mēket’ odyromenē kata thymon
aiōna phthinythō, posios potheousa philoio
pantoiēn aretēn, epei exochos ēen Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
Would that so soft a death Artemis the pure might give me
at once now, so that no longer lamenting in my heart
I may waste my life away, longing for my dear husband
for every kind of excellence, since he stood out among the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: If only Artemis the pure would give me so soft a death at once, now, so that I should no longer waste my life away lamenting in my heart, longing for my dear husband for every kind of excellence, since he stood out among the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: αἴθε is a particle of wish, ‘would that’, with πόροι the aorist optative of the defective aorist πόρον ‘give, furnish’. μαλακὸν θάνατον is ‘a soft death’, a gentle one. ἵνα takes the present subjunctive φθινύθω ‘waste away’, with αἰῶνα ‘life’ as object and ὀδυρομένη ‘lamenting’; κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in my heart’. ποθέουσα ‘longing for’ can be taken two ways: ‘longing for my dear husband, for every kind of excellence’ (as here, with πόσιος … φίλοιο the object and παντοίην ἀρετήν an accusative of respect), or ‘longing for every kind of excellence of my dear husband’, with πόσιος depending on ἀρετήν. ἔξοχος takes the genitive: ‘standing out among the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ὣς φαμένη κατέβαιν’ ὑπερώϊα σιγαλόεντα,
οὐκ οἴη·
sentences.tr:
hōs phamenē katebain’ hyperōïa sigaloenta,
ouk oiē·
sentences.l:
So saying, she came down the upper rooms, glossy,
not alone;
sentences.i: So saying, she came down from the glossy upper rooms, and not alone;
sentences.n: ὣς φαμένη is ‘so saying’, the participle of φημί. κατέβαιν’ is the imperfect κατέβαινε, ‘was coming down’. ὑπερώϊα is the plural of ὑπερώϊον, the upper rooms where the women live, here an accusative of the place she comes down from (English needs ‘from’), and σιγαλόεντα ‘glossy’ agrees with it. οὐκ οἴη is ‘not alone’, with the ano teleia after it, and the next unit says who went with her.

sentences.t: ἅμα τῇ γε καὶ ἀμφίπολοι δύ’ ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: hama tēi ge kai amphipoloi dy’ heponto.
sentences.l: with her, indeed, two handmaids also followed.
sentences.i: and two handmaids went with her.
sentences.n: ἅμα τῇ γε … ἕποντο is ‘with her, indeed, followed’, ἕποντο being the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ and δύ’ being δύο ‘two’. τῇ is ‘her’, the article as a pronoun. ἀμφίπολοι ‘handmaids’ are women who attend a lady, and the two mentioned here are the ones who stand on either hand of her at 211. The half-line ends at a full stop, and the Greek begins a new sentence at the next word.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὅτε δὴ μνηστῆρας ἀφίκετο δῖα γυναικῶν,
στῆ ῥα παρὰ σταθμὸν τέγεος πύκα ποιητοῖο,
ἄντα παρειάων σχομένη λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ hote dē mnēstēras aphiketo dia gynaikōn,
stē rha para stathmon tegeos pyka poiētoio,
anta pareiaōn schomenē lipara krēdemna·
sentences.i: When she reached the suitors, she, heavenly among women, stood by the doorpost of the well-built hall, holding her shining veil before her cheeks;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ ὅτε δὴ … ἀφίκετο is ‘and she, when now she reached’, and δῖα γυναικῶν ‘heavenly among women’ answers δῖα θεάων. στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι; σταθμός is the doorpost and τέγεος ‘of the roof’, with πύκα ποιητοῖο ‘closely built’. ἄντα παρειάων is ‘before her cheeks’, σχομένη ‘holding’, and λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα ‘shining veil’. These three lines are the same as 1.332–334 and, with a different first word, 16.414–416.

sentences.t: ἀμφίπολος δ’ ἄρα οἱ κεδνὴ ἑκάτερθε παρέστη.
sentences.tr: amphipolos d’ ara hoi kednē hekaterthe parestē.
sentences.l: and a trusty handmaid then, on each side of her, stood by.
sentences.i: and on either side of her a trusty handmaid took her stand.
sentences.n: ἀμφίπολος is ‘handmaid’, one for each side, so that the two of 207 stand on either hand of her. κεδνή is ‘trusty’, ἑκάτερθε ‘on each side’, with the ending -θε of place, and οἱ ‘her’. παρέστη is the aorist of παρίστημι, ‘stood beside’.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατ’, ἔρῳ δ’ ἄρα θυμὸν ἔθελχθεν,
πάντες δ’ ἠρήσαντο παραὶ λεχέεσσι κλιθῆναι.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ autou lyto gounat’, erōi d’ ara thymon ethelchthen,
pantes d’ ērēsanto parai lecheessi klithēnai.
sentences.l:
And of them on the spot their knees were loosed, and with desire their heart was enchanted,
and all of them prayed beside her to lie down.
sentences.i: Their knees gave way on the spot, and their hearts were enchanted with desire, and every one of them prayed to lie down at her side.
sentences.n: τῶν … λύτο γούνατ’ is ‘their knees were loosed’, λύτο being the unaugmented aorist passive of λύω, the stock expression for a sudden weakness. ἔρῳ is the dative of ἔρος ‘desire’, and ἔθελχθεν the aorist passive of θέλγω ‘enchant’, θυμόν being an accusative of respect, ‘in heart’. ἠρήσαντο is the aorist of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, with the infinitive κλιθῆναι ‘to lie down’; παραί is epic παρά, and λεχέεσσι the dative plural of λέχος ‘bed’, so ‘to lie beside her in bed’. The second line repeats 1.366.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχον προσεφώνεεν, ὃν φίλον υἱόν·
sentences.tr: hē d’ au Tēlemachon prosephōneen, hon philon huion·
sentences.l: And she in turn spoke to Telemachus, her own dear son:
sentences.i: And she in turn spoke to Telemachus, her own dear son:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction. ἡ δ’ αὖ is ‘and she in turn’, and προσεφώνεεν the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. ὃν φίλον υἱόν is ‘her own dear son’: ὅν here is the possessive ‘her own’, not the relative, and the phrase is in apposition to Τηλέμαχον. The speech itself begins in the next part, at 18.215, after the ano teleia.
